topics.name: Basic Components of Life
concepts: Amino acids join by peptide bonds (–CO–NH–) with loss of water [repeat]
Disaccharides: sucrose (glucose + fructose), maltose (glucose + glucose), lactose (glucose + galactose) [repeat]
Sucrose is non-reducing: both anomeric carbons are used in the glycosidic bond
Starch: α-glucose (α-1,4 + α-1,6); cellulose: β-1,4 glucose, unbranched
Oleic acid (C18:1) is unsaturated; stearic and palmitic acids are saturated [repeat]
Lipids dissolve in non-polar solvents (ether, chloroform), not in water [repeat]
Haemoglobin is a transport protein; keratin and collagen are structural proteins [repeat]
Protein levels: primary = sequence; secondary = α-helix/β-sheet; tertiary = 3-D fold; quaternary = subunits
Enzymes lower activation energy; they do not change ΔG or equilibrium
Coenzyme: loosely bound organic cofactor; prosthetic group: tightly bound
Lock-and-key: Fischer; induced fit: Koshland; Km = [S] at Vmax/2
Competitive inhibitor resembles substrate: malonate vs succinate dehydrogenase
Mg in chlorophyll; Fe in cytochromes; Mo in nitrogenase and nitrate reductase; Zn in carbonic anhydrase

topics.name: Cell Biology
concepts: Prokaryote: naked circular DNA in nucleoid, 70S ribosomes, no membrane organelles [repeat]
Cell theory: Schleiden & Schwann; 'omnis cellula e cellula': Virchow
Huxley: protoplasm is the physical basis of life [repeat]
Fluid mosaic model: Singer & Nicolson (1972); exocytosis releases vesicle contents outside [repeat]
Middle lamella: Ca and Mg pectate; plasmodesmata link neighbouring cells
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous: own DNA and 70S ribosomes [repeat]
Marker enzymes: succinate dehydrogenase (mitochondria), acid phosphatase (lysosome), catalase (peroxisome) [repeat]
Ribosome and centriole lack a membrane; ribosome = rRNA + protein; 70S = 50S + 30S, 80S = 60S + 40S [repeat]
SER: lipid/steroid synthesis; RER: protein synthesis; Golgi: glycosylation and packaging; lysosome: suicidal bag
Centromere: metacentric V, submetacentric L, acrocentric J, telocentric I (rod) [repeat]
Satellite lies beyond secondary constriction; nucleolar organiser sits at secondary constriction [repeat]
Prophase I order: leptotene, zygotene (synapsis), pachytene (crossing over, bivalent = 4 chromatids), diplotene, diakinesis [repeat]
Homologues separate at anaphase I; sister chromatids at anaphase II [repeat]
Cell plate forms from Golgi vesicles at the phragmoplast [repeat]
Mitosis keeps chromosome number and gives identical cells; meiosis halves it and gives variation [repeat]
Cell cycle: G1 → S (DNA replication) → G2 → M; non-dividing cells sit in G0

topics.name: Genetics
concepts: Central dogma: DNA → mRNA (transcription) → protein (translation); RNA → DNA is reverse transcription [repeat]
RNA has uracil and ribose; DNA has thymine and deoxyribose [repeat]
Chargaff: A = T, G = C, so (A+G)/(T+C) = 1 [repeat]
Genetic code: triplet, universal, degenerate, non-overlapping; AUG start; UAA, UAG, UGA stop [repeat]
Replication is semi-conservative (Meselson & Stahl); Okazaki fragments on lagging strand, joined by ligase [repeat]
Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate [repeat]
Test cross Tt × tt gives 1:1; dihybrid test cross gives 1:1:1:1 [repeat]
Tall × tall giving 3:1 means both parents heterozygous [repeat]
Incomplete dominance: F2 phenotypic = genotypic ratio 1:2:1 (Mirabilis) [repeat]
ABO: three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i); Iᴬ and Iᴮ codominant, both dominant over i [repeat]
Gamete types = 2ⁿ, n = number of heterozygous gene pairs [repeat]
Complete linkage gives only parental types; crossing over gives recombinants; 1% recombination = 1 map unit [repeat]
Colour blindness and haemophilia: X-linked recessive, criss-cross inheritance [repeat]
Benzer: cistron = unit of function, recon = recombination, muton = mutation [repeat]
Down: trisomy 21; Edward: trisomy 18; Patau: trisomy 13; Turner: 45,XO; Klinefelter: 47,XXY [repeat]
Kappa particles in Paramecium: cytoplasmic inheritance [repeat]

topics.name: Plant Physiology
concepts: DPD = OP − TP; fully turgid cell has DPD zero; water moves to higher DPD (lower Ψw)
Ψw = Ψs + Ψp; pure water Ψw = 0; excess fertiliser causes exosmosis and wilting [repeat]
Ascent of sap: cohesion–tension theory (Dixon & Joly); guttation through hydathodes
Stomata open by K⁺ influx into guard cells; ABA closes them
Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red most, reflects green; action spectrum = rate vs wavelength [repeat]
PS I: P700; PS II: P680; O₂ comes from photolysis of water at PS II [repeat]
Cyclic photophosphorylation: only ATP, no NADPH, no O₂ [repeat]
C3 first stable product 3-PGA; one glucose needs 18 ATP + 12 NADPH [repeat]
C4: PEP is the CO₂ acceptor, OAA first product, Kranz anatomy [repeat]
Photorespiration involves chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion
Glycolysis in cytoplasm, net 2 ATP + 2 NADH; link reaction is oxidative decarboxylation [repeat]
Krebs: 2 turns/glucose, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP; first product citric acid
Cytochromes carry electrons in both photosynthesis and respiration; O₂ is the final acceptor in ETS [repeat]
RQ: carbohydrate 1, fat ≈ 0.7, organic acids > 1, anaerobic infinite
Gibberellin: bolting, malting (α-amylase); cytokinin: delays senescence, breaks apical dominance [repeat]
Auxin: apical dominance, rooting (IBA), 2,4-D weedicide; epigeal: hypocotyl grows, hypogeal: epicotyl grows

topics.name: Developmental Botany
concepts: Autogamy: same flower; geitonogamy: another flower of same plant; xenogamy: another plant [repeat]
Cleistogamous flowers never open, so they are always self-pollinated [repeat]
Protandry: anthers mature first (sunflower); protogyny: stigma matures first [repeat]
Microspore mother cell → 4 microspores (pollen); usually shed at 2-celled stage
Tapetum is the innermost anther wall layer that nourishes developing pollen [repeat]
Embryo sac develops from the functional (chalazal) megaspore; 7-celled, 8-nucleate [repeat]
Double fertilisation (Nawaschin): syngamy + triple fusion; 5 nuclei involved
Angiosperm endosperm is triploid (2 polar nuclei + 1 male gamete); gymnosperm endosperm is haploid [repeat]
Endosperm ploidy = 2 × (female gamete ploidy) + male gamete ploidy [repeat]
Coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm; pea and gram seeds are non-endospermic
Monocot embryo: scutellum (cotyledon), coleoptile covers plumule, coleorhiza covers radicle
Banana is propagated by suckers; apomixis = seed without fertilisation [repeat]

questions.q: The lock-and-key model of enzyme action was proposed by
questions.x: Fischer (1894) proposed the rigid lock-and-key model; Koshland later proposed the induced-fit model.
questions.trap: Koshland is picked by confusing induced fit with lock-and-key.

questions.q: Malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase. This is an example of
questions.x: Malonate resembles succinate in structure and competes for the same active site.

questions.q: Km (Michaelis constant) of an enzyme is the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is
questions.x: By definition, at [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2. A low Km means high affinity for substrate.

questions.q: Cellulose is a polymer of
o: α-D-glucose joined by α-1,4 glycosidic bonds
β-D-glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds
questions.x: Cellulose is an unbranched chain of β-glucose with β-1,4 links; starch uses α-glucose.
questions.trap: α-1,4 is starch (amylose), not cellulose.

questions.q: Enzymes that remove groups from substrates by a mechanism other than hydrolysis, leaving a double bond, are
questions.x: Lyases (e.g. aldolase, fumarase) break bonds without water, forming double bonds; hydrolases use water.
questions.trap: Ligases sound similar but join molecules using ATP.

questions.q: Molybdenum is essential for the activity of
questions.x: Mo is a component of nitrogenase and nitrate reductase in nitrogen metabolism.
questions.trap: Carbonic anhydrase needs zinc, not molybdenum.

questions.q: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was given by
questions.x: Singer and Nicolson (1972): lipid bilayer with proteins floating in it.
questions.trap: Danielli–Davson gave the older sandwich model.

questions.q: The 70S ribosome of a prokaryote is made of subunits
questions.x: Svedberg units are not additive; 50S + 30S form 70S.
questions.trap: 60S + 40S is the eukaryotic 80S ribosome.

questions.q: Which organelle is semi-autonomous?
questions.x: Mitochondria (like chloroplasts) have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes.

questions.q: The glyoxylate cycle, which converts fats into carbohydrates in germinating oily seeds, occurs in
questions.x: Glyoxysomes are specialised microbodies in fatty seeds (e.g. castor) containing isocitrate lyase and malate synthase.
questions.trap: Leaf peroxisomes are involved in photorespiration, not the glyoxylate cycle.

questions.q: Crossing over takes place during
questions.x: Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids occurs at pachytene.
questions.trap: Diplotene is chosen because chiasmata become visible then.

questions.q: Synaptonemal complex is formed during
questions.x: Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) at zygotene, held by the synaptonemal complex.
questions.trap: Pachytene/diplotene is confused with synapsis.

questions.q: In mitosis, the centromere splits and sister chromatids move apart during
questions.x: At anaphase the centromeres divide and chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.

questions.q: If a meiocyte has 2C DNA in G1, the DNA content of each daughter cell at the end of meiosis I is
questions.x: S phase doubles 2C to 4C; meiosis I halves it, so each cell has 2C. Meiosis II gives 1C.
questions.trap: 1C is picked because chromosome number halves in meiosis I.

questions.q: Minimum number of meiotic divisions needed to produce 100 seeds in an angiosperm is
questions.x: 100 megaspore mother cells need 100 meioses; 100 pollen grains need 25 meioses (4 per meiosis). 100 + 25 = 125.
questions.trap: 100 forgets the pollen; 200 counts one meiosis per pollen.

questions.q: Cell A has Ψs = −0.8 MPa and Ψp = +0.3 MPa; cell B has Ψs = −0.6 MPa and Ψp = +0.3 MPa. Water will move
o: Equally in both directions with no net flow
From A to B and then back
questions.x: Ψw(A) = −0.8 + 0.3 = −0.5 MPa; Ψw(B) = −0.6 + 0.3 = −0.3 MPa. Water flows to lower Ψw, so B → A.
questions.trap: Picking A → B by comparing Ψs magnitudes the wrong way.

questions.q: Opening of stomata is associated with
o: Efflux of K⁺ ions from guard cells
Influx of K⁺ ions into guard cells
Conversion of sugar into starch in guard cells
Rise of abscisic acid in guard cells
questions.x: K⁺ (with malate) enters guard cells, lowers Ψw, water enters, cells turn turgid and the pore opens.
questions.trap: ABA closes stomata, not opens them.

questions.q: Photolysis of water and evolution of oxygen are associated with
questions.x: The oxygen-evolving complex is on the PS II side; cyclic flow involves only PS I and releases no O₂.

questions.q: The reaction centre of photosystem I is
questions.x: PS I has P700; PS II has P680.
questions.trap: P680 belongs to PS II.

questions.q: The primary CO₂ acceptor in mesophyll cells of C4 plants is
questions.x: PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ onto PEP forming oxaloacetate, the first stable product.
questions.trap: OAA is the first product, not the acceptor.

questions.q: To synthesise one molecule of glucose through the Calvin cycle, the ATP and NADPH required are
questions.x: Each CO₂ needs 3 ATP + 2 NADPH; glucose needs 6 CO₂: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
questions.trap: Swapping the numbers (12 ATP, 18 NADPH).

questions.q: Photorespiration involves the cooperation of
questions.x: RuBisCO oxygenation in chloroplast forms glycolate; it is processed in peroxisome and glycine to serine in mitochondrion.
questions.trap: Glyoxysome is confused with peroxisome.

questions.q: Number of NADH produced in the Krebs cycle (excluding the link reaction) from one molecule of glucose is
questions.x: One glucose gives 2 acetyl-CoA; each turn yields 3 NADH, so 2 × 3 = 6.
questions.trap: 3 counts only one turn; 8 adds the link reaction's 2 NADH.

questions.q: Respiratory quotient is less than one when the respiratory substrate is
questions.x: Fats are poor in oxygen, so O₂ used exceeds CO₂ released (tripalmitin RQ ≈ 0.7).
questions.trap: Organic acids give RQ more than one.

questions.q: Bolting (sudden stem elongation before flowering) in rosette plants such as cabbage is caused by
questions.x: Gibberellins cause internode elongation and bolting in rosette plants.

questions.q: In a short-day plant kept on a short-day cycle, flowering is prevented if the long dark period is interrupted by a brief flash of
questions.x: Red light converts Pr to Pfr, breaking the critical dark period; far-red given after it reverses the effect.
questions.trap: Far-red reverses the night-break; it does not cause it.
questions.s: Plant growth (photoperiodism; not named in 2026 syllabus)

questions.q: A dihybrid test cross (AaBb × aabb) gives the phenotypic ratio
questions.x: AaBb forms 4 gamete types equally; aabb contributes only ab, so four phenotypes 1:1:1:1.
questions.trap: 9:3:3:1 is the F2 selfing ratio.

questions.q: In a monohybrid cross showing incomplete dominance (e.g. Mirabilis jalapa), the F2 phenotypic ratio is
questions.x: Heterozygotes are intermediate (pink), so red:pink:white = 1:2:1.
questions.trap: 3:1 applies only to complete dominance.

questions.q: Two white-flowered varieties of sweet pea crossed give purple F1. On selfing F1, the F2 ratio of purple to white is
questions.x: Complementary genes: purple needs both dominant C and P; 9 C_P_ purple, 7 white.
questions.trap: 9:3:4 is recessive epistasis.

questions.q: Test cross of AB/ab gave AB 420, ab 430, Ab 75 and aB 75. The distance between genes A and B is
questions.trap: 7.5 uses only one recombinant class.

questions.q: XX-female / XY-male sex determination in plants is found in
questions.x: Melandrium is dioecious; males are XY and females XX. Pea, maize and rice have no sex chromosomes.

questions.q: Colchicine induces polyploidy because it
questions.x: Without a spindle, duplicated chromosomes cannot separate, so the chromosome set doubles.

questions.q: Insertion or deletion of a single base in the coding region of a gene causes
questions.x: The reading frame of triplets shifts from that point onward.
questions.trap: Transition/transversion are substitutions, not insertions.
questions.s: Concept and types (gene and chromosomal mutations)

questions.q: A DNA segment of 1000 base pairs contains 300 adenine. The total number of hydrogen bonds in it is
questions.x: A–T pairs = 300 (2 bonds each = 600); G–C pairs = 700 (3 bonds each = 2100); total 2700.
questions.trap: 2300 swaps 2 and 3 bonds between the pair types.
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA

questions.q: The semi-conservative mode of DNA replication was experimentally proved by
questions.x: Meselson and Stahl (1958) grew E. coli in ¹⁵N then ¹⁴N and separated DNA by density.
questions.trap: Watson and Crick proposed the model but did not prove it.

questions.q: Which codon is NOT a stop codon?
questions.x: UGG codes for tryptophan; UAA, UAG and UGA are termination codons.
questions.trap: UGA looks like UGG but is a stop codon.

questions.q: In eukaryotes, mRNA (hnRNA) is transcribed by
questions.x: Pol I makes rRNA, Pol II makes hnRNA/mRNA, Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.

questions.q: Adjacent amino acids in a polypeptide chain are linked by
questions.x: The –COOH of one amino acid joins the –NH₂ of the next with loss of water, forming a –CO–NH– peptide bond.
questions.trap: Glycosidic bonds link sugars, not amino acids.

questions.q: Which pair consists only of disaccharides?
questions.x: Sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose) are disaccharides; glucose, fructose, ribose, galactose are monosaccharides.
questions.trap: Starch and glycogen are polysaccharides.

questions.q: Oleic acid differs from stearic acid in that oleic acid
o: Has one C=C double bond in its chain
questions.x: Both are C18 fatty acids; oleic acid (C18:1) has one cis double bond, so it is unsaturated and liquid at room temperature; stearic acid is saturated.
questions.trap: Students call oleic acid saturated because it is common in fats.

questions.q: Lipids are generally
o: Insoluble in water but soluble in ether and chloroform
Soluble in water but insoluble in ether
Equally soluble in water and ether
Insoluble in both water and organic solvents
questions.x: Lipids are non-polar (hydrophobic), so they dissolve in non-polar organic solvents and not in water.

questions.q: Which of the following is a transport protein?
questions.x: Haemoglobin carries O₂; keratin and collagen are structural proteins; insulin is a hormone.

questions.q: A non-protein organic cofactor that is loosely attached to the apoenzyme is called
questions.x: Coenzymes (e.g. NAD⁺) bind loosely; prosthetic groups (e.g. haem) bind tightly; apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme.
questions.trap: Prosthetic group is also organic but tightly bound.

questions.q: Magnesium is a structural component of
questions.x: Mg²⁺ sits at the centre of the porphyrin ring of chlorophyll; cytochromes contain iron.
questions.trap: Cytochromes have an iron (haem) centre, not magnesium.

questions.q: The α-helix and β-pleated sheet of a protein are features of its
questions.x: Secondary structure is local folding held by hydrogen bonds; primary is the amino acid sequence.

questions.q: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because
o: The reducing groups of both glucose and fructose are used in the glycosidic bond
questions.x: The bond joins C1 of glucose to C2 of fructose, so no free aldehyde or ketone group is left to reduce Benedict's reagent.
questions.trap: Maltose and lactose keep one free reducing end; sucrose does not.

questions.q: Enzymes increase the rate of a reaction by
questions.x: Enzymes provide an alternative path with lower activation energy; ΔG and equilibrium are unchanged.

questions.q: Mitochondria are called semi-autonomous because they
o: Have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes but depend on nuclear genes for most proteins
Divide only when the nucleus divides
Make all of their own proteins
questions.x: Mitochondrial DNA codes for a few proteins; most mitochondrial proteins are coded by nuclear genes and imported.
questions.trap: 'Autonomous' would mean making all their own proteins.

questions.q: The marker enzyme of mitochondria is
questions.x: Succinate dehydrogenase sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Acid phosphatase marks lysosomes, catalase peroxisomes, glucose-6-phosphatase ER.

questions.q: The genetic material of a bacterial cell is
o: Linear DNA wound on histones inside a nucleus
Linear DNA enclosed by a nuclear envelope
A naked circular DNA lying in the nucleoid
questions.x: Prokaryotes lack a nuclear membrane; their single circular DNA (without true histones) lies in the nucleoid region.

questions.q: Which pair of cell organelles is NOT bounded by a membrane?
questions.x: Ribosomes (rRNA + protein) and centrioles (microtubules) have no membrane; mitochondria and chloroplasts have two.

questions.q: Ribosomes are chemically made of
questions.x: Each ribosomal subunit is a complex of rRNA and many proteins (ribonucleoprotein).

questions.q: Release of secretory material from a cell when vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane is
questions.x: In exocytosis, vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane and the contents are discharged outside.
questions.trap: Pinocytosis takes fluid in, not out.

questions.q: Protoplasm was described as 'the physical basis of life' by
questions.x: Huxley (1868) called protoplasm the physical basis of life. Hooke named cells; Brown discovered the nucleus.

questions.q: At anaphase, a telocentric chromosome appears
questions.x: With the centromere at the tip, there is only one arm, so it is pulled as a rod. Metacentric is V, submetacentric L.
questions.trap: V-shape belongs to metacentric chromosomes.

questions.q: A chromosome with its centromere exactly in the middle and two equal arms is
questions.x: Metacentric = median centromere, equal arms; submetacentric slightly off-centre; acrocentric near the end; telocentric at the end.

questions.q: The knob-like part of a chromosome beyond the secondary constriction is the
questions.x: A chromosome bearing a satellite is a SAT chromosome; the secondary constriction there is the nucleolar organiser.
questions.trap: Telomere is the tip of every chromosome, not this knob.

questions.q: The nucleolar organiser region of a chromosome is located at the
questions.x: rRNA genes at the secondary constriction (NOR) organise the nucleolus; the primary constriction is the centromere.

questions.q: Homologous chromosomes separate from each other during
questions.x: Disjunction of homologues occurs at anaphase I, halving the chromosome number; chromatids separate at anaphase II.
questions.trap: Anaphase II separates sister chromatids, not homologues.

questions.q: Sister chromatids move to opposite poles in meiosis during
questions.x: Centromeres split only at anaphase II; in anaphase I each homologue still has two chromatids joined at the centromere.

questions.q: Cell plate formation in a dividing plant cell is initiated by vesicles derived from
questions.x: Golgi vesicles collect at the phragmoplast and fuse to form the cell plate, which becomes the middle lamella.
questions.trap: Plant cells have no centrioles.

questions.q: A bivalent at pachytene contains
questions.x: Two paired homologues, each with 2 sister chromatids on one centromere: 4 chromatids (a tetrad) and 2 centromeres.
questions.trap: Counting one centromere per chromatid gives 4.

questions.q: A feature of mitosis that distinguishes it from meiosis is that mitosis
o: Keeps the chromosome number and gives genetically identical cells
questions.x: Mitosis is equational: daughter cells are identical to the parent. Synapsis, crossing over and four cells belong to meiosis.

questions.q: 'Omnis cellula e cellula' (every cell arises from a pre-existing cell) was given by
questions.x: Virchow (1855) added this to the cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann.
questions.trap: Schleiden and Schwann gave the original cell theory.

questions.q: The middle lamella is mainly composed of
questions.x: The middle lamella cements adjacent cells together with Ca and Mg pectates.
questions.trap: Cellulose is the main component of primary and secondary walls.

questions.q: Cytoplasmic strands that connect adjacent plant cells through their walls are
questions.x: Plasmodesmata pass through the cell walls and form the symplast; desmosomes are animal cell junctions.

questions.q: Lysosomes are called 'suicidal bags' because they
o: Contain hydrolytic enzymes that can digest the cell itself
questions.x: Rupture of lysosomes releases acid hydrolases that cause autolysis of the cell.

questions.q: Glycosylation of proteins and packaging of secretory products mainly occur in the
questions.x: Golgi cisternae modify proteins from the RER (glycosylation) and pack them into vesicles.

questions.q: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is mainly concerned with synthesis of
questions.x: SER lacks ribosomes and makes lipids/steroids; RER bears ribosomes and makes proteins.
questions.trap: Protein synthesis is the job of rough ER.

questions.q: In a chloroplast, the enzymes of the Calvin cycle are located in the
questions.x: Light reactions occur on thylakoid membranes; CO₂ fixation (RuBisCO and Calvin enzymes) occurs in the stroma.

questions.q: The axoneme of a eukaryotic flagellum shows microtubules arranged as
questions.x: Nine peripheral doublets surround two central singlets; the basal body has a 9 + 0 triplet pattern.
questions.trap: 9 + 0 is the basal body/centriole.

questions.q: Direct division of the nucleus without formation of spindle or chromosomes is
questions.x: In amitosis the nucleus simply elongates and constricts into two (e.g. some algae, yeast).

questions.q: DNA replication takes place in which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.x: DNA content doubles (2C → 4C) in the synthesis (S) phase of interphase.

questions.q: Cells that permanently stop dividing, such as mature nerve cells, remain in
questions.x: Cells exit G1 into the quiescent G0 stage and stay metabolically active without dividing.

questions.q: Terminalisation of chiasmata is completed during
questions.x: Chiasmata appear at diplotene and move to the chromosome ends, finishing at diakinesis.
questions.trap: Diplotene is when chiasmata first become visible.

questions.q: A root-tip cell has 2n = 16. The number of chromatids at metaphase of mitosis is
questions.x: Each of the 16 chromosomes has two sister chromatids at metaphase: 16 × 2 = 32.
questions.trap: 16 counts chromosomes, not chromatids.

questions.q: Synthesis of DNA on an RNA template is called
questions.x: Reverse transcriptase (found in retroviruses) copies RNA into DNA, the reverse of transcription.
questions.trap: Transcription is DNA → RNA.

questions.q: The step mRNA → polypeptide in the central dogma is
questions.x: Translation decodes mRNA codons into an amino acid chain on ribosomes.

questions.q: Which nitrogen base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.x: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine; A, G and C occur in both.
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
questions.trap: Thymine is the DNA-only base.

questions.q: Where the DNA template strand has adenine, the base placed in the mRNA during transcription is
questions.x: RNA polymerase pairs A on DNA with U in RNA, because RNA has no thymine.
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
questions.trap: Thymine would be correct only in DNA replication.

questions.q: A double-stranded DNA has 30% guanine. The percentage of thymine is
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
questions.trap: 40% is A + T together, not thymine alone.

questions.q: In any double-stranded DNA, which ratio is always equal to one?
questions.x: Since A = T and G = C, purines = pyrimidines, so (A + G)/(T + C) = 1. (A + T)/(G + C) varies by species.
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
questions.trap: (A + T)/(G + C) is species-specific, not 1.

questions.q: A bacterium can make a human protein from an inserted human gene because the genetic code is
questions.x: The same codons specify the same amino acids in nearly all organisms, so genes work across species.

questions.q: Okazaki fragments are formed on
o: The leading strand during DNA replication
The lagging strand during DNA replication
questions.x: DNA polymerase works only 5' → 3', so the strand running the other way is copied in short pieces (Okazaki fragments).
questions.trap: The leading strand is made continuously.

questions.q: The enzyme that joins Okazaki fragments is
questions.x: Ligase seals the nicks between fragments; helicase unwinds, primase makes RNA primers.

questions.q: A nucleotide differs from a nucleoside in having
questions.x: Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate.
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA

questions.q: A monohybrid test cross (Tt × tt) gives the phenotypic ratio
questions.x: Tt gives T and t gametes equally; tt gives only t, so Tt : tt = 1 : 1.
questions.trap: 3 : 1 comes from selfing Tt, not test crossing.

questions.q: Two tall pea plants are crossed and one-fourth of the offspring are dwarf. The parents are
questions.x: Dwarf (tt) appears in 1/4 only when both parents carry t: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.
questions.trap: Tt × tt gives half dwarf, not one-fourth.

questions.q: In which type of inheritance are the F2 phenotypic and genotypic ratios the same?
questions.x: With incomplete dominance the heterozygote has its own phenotype, so both ratios are 1 : 2 : 1.
questions.trap: Complete dominance gives 3 : 1 phenotypic but 1 : 2 : 1 genotypic.

questions.q: The ABO blood group in humans is controlled by
o: Two alleles of a single gene
Three alleles of a single gene
questions.x: One gene (I) has three alleles: Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i (multiple alleles); a person carries any two.
questions.trap: Three blood antigens make students think of three genes.

questions.q: A man heterozygous for blood group A (Iᴬi) marries a woman heterozygous for group B (Iᴮi). The chance that their child has group O is
questions.x: Child is ii only if each parent passes i: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Children can be AB, A, B or O, each 1/4.
questions.trap: 0 is chosen by thinking A and B parents cannot have an O child.

questions.q: A person of blood group AB shows both A and B antigens on red cells. This is an example of
questions.x: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both fully expressed in the heterozygote: co-dominance. Incomplete dominance would give a blend.
questions.trap: Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate, not both traits.

questions.q: How many kinds of gametes are produced by a plant of genotype AaBbCcDD?
questions.x: Only three gene pairs are heterozygous: 2³ = 8. DD gives only D.
questions.trap: 16 wrongly counts DD as heterozygous.

questions.q: An organism carrying two identical alleles of a gene (e.g. TT or tt) is
questions.x: Homozygous = identical alleles; heterozygous (hybrid) = different alleles (Tt).

questions.q: When genes lie so close that only parental combinations appear in the progeny, it is called
questions.x: No crossing over occurs between them, so recombinants are absent (e.g. male Drosophila).

questions.q: Crossing over is significant mainly because it
questions.x: Exchange between non-sister chromatids recombines alleles, adding variation; it is also used to map genes.
questions.s: Concept and significance of crossing over

questions.q: A colour-blind man marries a woman with normal vision whose father was colour-blind. The chance that any son of theirs is colour-blind is
questions.x: Woman is a carrier (XᶜX). Sons take their X from the mother, so half the sons get Xᶜ: 50%.
questions.trap: 25% is the chance of a colour-blind son among all children.

questions.q: A white-eyed female Drosophila (XʷXʷ) is crossed with a red-eyed male (XᵂY). The F1 males are
questions.x: Sons get their only X from the mother (Xʷ), so all are white-eyed; daughters (XᵂXʷ) are red: criss-cross inheritance.
questions.trap: Students assume sons resemble the father.

questions.q: Haemophilia in humans is inherited as
questions.x: The gene is on the X chromosome and recessive, so males (XʰY) are mostly affected.

questions.q: Kappa particles transmitted through the cytoplasm of Paramecium illustrate
questions.x: Kappa particles in the cytoplasm pass on the 'killer' trait without following Mendelian nuclear ratios.

questions.q: According to Benzer, the cistron, recon and muton are units of, respectively,
questions.x: Cistron codes one polypeptide (function); recon is the smallest unit of recombination; muton the smallest unit that can mutate.

questions.q: The ultimate source of new genetic variation is
questions.x: Only mutation creates new alleles; recombination reshuffles existing ones; selection acts on variation.
questions.trap: Recombination reshuffles alleles but does not create new ones.

questions.q: Replacement of a purine by a pyrimidine in DNA is called
questions.x: Transversion: purine ⇄ pyrimidine. Transition: purine → purine or pyrimidine → pyrimidine.
questions.s: Concept and types (gene and chromosomal mutations)
questions.trap: Transition is the same-class swap.

questions.q: Down's syndrome is caused by
o: An extra X chromosome in males
questions.x: Down's syndrome is 47, +21. XO is Turner's, XXY is Klinefelter's, trisomy 18 is Edward's.

questions.q: The karyotype 45, XO (44 + XO) is found in
questions.x: Turner's females lack one X (monosomy); Klinefelter's males are 47, XXY.
questions.trap: Klinefelter's also involves sex chromosomes but has an extra X.

questions.q: Edward's syndrome is due to trisomy of chromosome
questions.x: Edward's = trisomy 18; Patau's = trisomy 13; Down's = trisomy 21.
questions.trap: 13 is Patau's syndrome.

questions.q: Which disorder is caused by a gene mutation rather than a change in chromosome number?
questions.x: Albinism is an autosomal recessive gene defect (no melanin); the others are aneuploidies.

questions.q: Triticale, the first man-made cereal, is
o: An allopolyploid of wheat and rye
questions.x: Triticale combines chromosome sets of wheat (Triticum) and rye (Secale) and is doubled to be fertile: allopolyploid.

questions.q: In Mendel's dihybrid F2 (AaBb × AaBb), the number of the 16 combinations that are homozygous for both genes is
questions.x: AABB, AAbb, aaBB and aabb: 4 of 16.
questions.trap: 1 counts only the double recessive.

questions.q: Excess chemical fertiliser around the roots makes a plant wilt because
o: Roots absorb too much water and burst
The soil solution becomes hypertonic and water leaves root cells
questions.x: A concentrated soil solution has lower water potential than root cells, so water moves out (exosmosis) and cells plasmolyse.
questions.s: Water relations: osmosis and its types, plasmolysis

questions.q: Shrinkage of the protoplast away from the cell wall in a hypertonic solution is
questions.x: Water leaves by exosmosis and the protoplast pulls away from the wall; deplasmolysis is the reverse in water.
questions.s: Water relations: osmosis and its types, plasmolysis

questions.q: The diffusion pressure deficit (DPD) of a fully turgid cell is
o: Equal to twice its turgor pressure
questions.x: DPD = OP − TP; at full turgor TP = OP, so DPD = 0 and the cell takes in no more water.
questions.trap: Maximum DPD is for a flaccid cell (TP = 0).

questions.q: The water potential of pure water at atmospheric pressure is
questions.x: Pure water is the reference with Ψw = 0; adding solutes makes Ψw negative.

questions.q: A cell has osmotic pressure 12 atm and turgor pressure 4 atm. Its DPD is
questions.x: DPD = OP − TP = 12 − 4 = 8 atm.
questions.trap: 16 adds the pressures instead of subtracting.

questions.q: Swelling of dry seeds when soaked in water is mainly due to
questions.x: Hydrophilic colloids (proteins, cellulose, starch) adsorb water and swell; imbibition precedes germination.

questions.q: Loss of water in liquid form through hydathodes at leaf margins is
questions.x: Guttation occurs at night or early morning under high root pressure; transpiration loses water as vapour.

questions.q: The most widely accepted theory of ascent of sap in tall trees is the
questions.x: Dixon and Joly: transpiration pull plus cohesion of water molecules lifts the xylem column.
questions.trap: Root pressure is too small to lift water up tall trees.

questions.q: Chlorophyll a absorbs light most strongly in the
questions.x: Its absorption spectrum peaks near 430 nm (blue) and 662 nm (red); green light is reflected.
questions.trap: Leaves look green because green is reflected, not absorbed.

questions.q: A graph showing the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths of light is called the
questions.x: Absorption spectrum shows light absorbed by a pigment; action spectrum shows the photosynthetic rate.
questions.trap: Absorption spectrum plots absorbance, not rate.

questions.q: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from
questions.x: Ruben and Kamen used ¹⁸O to show that O₂ comes from photolysis of water at photosystem II.
questions.trap: CO₂ is chosen because it contains oxygen too.

questions.q: The Calvin cycle is called the C₃ cycle because
o: Its first stable product, 3-phosphoglycerate, has three carbons
It uses three ATP per CO₂
Its CO₂ acceptor has three carbons
questions.x: RuBisCO joins CO₂ to RuBP (5C) to give two molecules of 3-PGA (3C), the first stable product.
questions.trap: RuBP, the acceptor, has five carbons, not three.

questions.q: Photophosphorylation means
o: Synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi using light energy
questions.x: Light-driven electron flow builds a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase: ADP + Pi → ATP.

questions.q: Cyclic photophosphorylation produces
questions.x: Only PS I works and electrons return to it, so no water splits (no O₂) and no NADP⁺ is reduced.
questions.trap: Non-cyclic flow makes ATP, NADPH and O₂.

questions.q: Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is an example of
questions.x: Pyruvate loses CO₂ (decarboxylation) and is oxidised as NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
questions.trap: Carboxylation adds CO₂; here CO₂ is removed.

questions.q: Which stage of aerobic respiration takes place outside the mitochondria?
questions.x: Glycolysis runs in the cytoplasm (cytosol); the rest occur in the mitochondrial matrix or inner membrane.

questions.q: Net gain of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis of one glucose is
questions.x: 4 ATP are made but 2 are used in the early steps, so the net gain is 2 ATP (plus 2 NADH).
questions.trap: 4 is the gross, not the net.

questions.q: In alcoholic fermentation by yeast, pyruvic acid is converted into
questions.x: Pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde, which is reduced to ethanol; CO₂ is released.
questions.trap: Lactic acid is formed in muscle, not yeast.

questions.q: The final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial electron transport system is
questions.x: Cytochrome oxidase passes electrons to O₂, which takes up H⁺ to form water.
questions.s: Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation

questions.q: The respiratory quotient of anaerobic respiration is
questions.x: RQ = CO₂ released / O₂ used; CO₂ is released but no O₂ is used, so RQ is infinite.
questions.trap: Zero would need no CO₂ release.

questions.q: Cytochromes act as electron carriers in
questions.x: Cytochrome b₆f links PS II and PS I in chloroplasts; cytochromes b, c, a, a₃ work in the mitochondrial ETS.
questions.s: Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation

questions.q: In malting of barley, gibberellin acts by
o: Inducing α-amylase synthesis in the aleurone layer
questions.x: GA from the embryo signals the aleurone layer to make α-amylase, which digests endosperm starch into sugars.

questions.q: Cut flowers and leafy vegetables stay fresh longer when sprayed with
questions.x: Cytokinins delay senescence by keeping protein and chlorophyll from breaking down (Richmond–Lang effect).
questions.trap: Ethylene speeds up senescence and ripening.

questions.q: The hormone that promotes growth of lateral buds and so counteracts apical dominance is
questions.x: Auxin from the apex suppresses lateral buds; cytokinin promotes their growth.
questions.trap: Auxin causes apical dominance; it does not counteract it.

questions.q: Apical dominance in plants is caused by
o: Auxin produced by the apical bud
questions.x: Auxin moving down from the shoot tip inhibits lateral bud growth; removing the apex releases them.

questions.q: 2,4-D is commonly used as
questions.x: At high concentration this synthetic auxin kills dicot weeds while cereals (monocots) are less affected.

questions.q: In hypogeal germination (e.g. pea), the cotyledons remain below the soil because
o: The epicotyl elongates while the hypocotyl does not
questions.x: In hypogeal germination the epicotyl pushes the plumule up; in epigeal (bean, castor) the hypocotyl lifts the cotyledons.
questions.trap: Hypocotyl elongation gives epigeal germination.

questions.q: Dormancy caused by a hard, impermeable seed coat is broken by
questions.x: Scratching or acid-treating the coat (scarification) lets water and O₂ in; ABA promotes dormancy.
questions.trap: ABA induces dormancy, not breaks it.

questions.q: Germination of seeds while still attached to the parent plant, as in Rhizophora, is
questions.x: Mangroves like Rhizophora show vivipary, an adaptation to saline, marshy soil.

questions.q: Kranz anatomy is characteristic of the leaves of
questions.x: Kranz anatomy: bundle sheath cells with many chloroplasts ringed by mesophyll, typical of C₄ plants (maize, sugarcane).

questions.q: Bacterial photosynthesis differs from plant photosynthesis in that bacteria
o: Do not release oxygen, as they use donors like H₂S instead of water
Use chlorophyll a and two photosystems
questions.x: Purple and green sulphur bacteria use bacteriochlorophyll and H₂S as the electron donor, so photosynthesis is anoxygenic.

questions.q: The first product formed in the Krebs cycle is
questions.x: Acetyl-CoA (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C) to form citric acid (6C), so it is also called the citric acid cycle.
questions.trap: Oxaloacetate is the acceptor, not the first product.

questions.q: Transfer of pollen from one flower to the stigma of another flower on the same plant is
questions.x: Geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination but genetically self-pollination; xenogamy is between different plants.
questions.trap: Xenogamy needs a different plant.

questions.q: Cleistogamous flowers ensure
questions.x: Cleistogamous flowers (e.g. Commelina, Viola, Oxalis) stay closed, so anthers shed pollen directly on the stigma.

questions.q: In sunflower the anthers mature before the stigma of the same flower is receptive. This condition is
questions.x: Protandry (anthers first) is a dichogamy that favours cross-pollination; protogyny is stigma first.
questions.trap: Protogyny is the reverse order.

questions.q: The endosperm of a typical angiosperm is
o: Triploid, formed by fusion of a male gamete with two polar nuclei
Diploid, formed by fusion of egg and male gamete
Haploid, formed from the female gametophyte
questions.x: Triple fusion (male gamete + secondary nucleus) gives the 3n primary endosperm nucleus.
questions.trap: 2n describes the zygote/embryo; haploid endosperm is in gymnosperms.

questions.q: A tetraploid (4n) plant is pollinated by a diploid (2n) plant. The ploidy of the embryo and endosperm will be
questions.x: Egg and each polar nucleus are 2n; male gamete is n. Embryo = 2n + n = 3n; endosperm = 2n + 2n + n = 5n.
questions.trap: 4n forgets that both polar nuclei come from the tetraploid mother.

questions.q: In which plant is the endosperm haploid?
questions.x: In gymnosperms the endosperm is the female gametophyte formed before fertilisation, so it is n.
questions.trap: Maize and coconut have triploid endosperm.

questions.q: The liquid endosperm of coconut (coconut water) is an example of
questions.x: Free nuclear divisions occur without walls; the white kernel is the cellular part.

questions.q: Seeds in which the endosperm is fully used up by the developing embryo, as in pea and gram, are called
questions.x: In pea and gram the cotyledons absorb the endosperm; castor and maize keep it (albuminous).

questions.q: The embryo sac (female gametophyte) of angiosperms develops from
questions.x: Of the four megaspores formed by meiosis, usually the chalazal one survives and forms the embryo sac.

questions.q: A mature Polygonum-type embryo sac is
questions.x: 3 antipodals + egg apparatus (egg + 2 synergids) + 1 central cell with 2 polar nuclei: 7 cells, 8 nuclei.
questions.trap: 8-celled forgets that the central cell has two nuclei.

questions.q: The main function of the tapetum in the anther is to
o: Help in dehiscence of the anther
Protect the anther from the outside
questions.x: The tapetum, the innermost wall layer, supplies food and materials (e.g. sporopollenin precursors) to pollen.
questions.trap: Endothecium, not tapetum, helps in dehiscence.

questions.q: Double fertilisation in angiosperms was discovered by
questions.x: Nawaschin (1898) observed it in Lilium and Fritillaria. Amici discovered the pollen tube.

questions.q: In a grass embryo, the single shield-shaped cotyledon is called the
questions.x: The scutellum absorbs food from the endosperm; the coleoptile sheathes the plumule, the coleorhiza the radicle.
questions.s: Structure of monocot and dicot embryo
questions.trap: Coleoptile is the plumule sheath.

questions.q: Banana is commonly propagated vegetatively by
questions.x: Suckers arise from the underground stem and grow into new plants; banana fruits are seedless.

questions.q: The number of pollen grains formed from one microspore mother cell is
questions.x: Each microspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to give a tetrad of 4 microspores (pollen).

questions.q: In most angiosperms, the pollen grain is shed at the
questions.x: In about 60–70% of species pollen is shed 2-celled; the generative cell divides later in the pollen tube.
questions.trap: 3-celled shedding occurs in fewer species (e.g. grasses).

questions.q: Formation of seeds without fertilisation is called
questions.x: Apomixis gives seeds asexually; parthenocarpy gives seedless fruit without fertilisation.
questions.trap: Parthenocarpy produces fruit, not seeds.

questions.q: A cell with Ψs = −1.0 MPa and Ψp = +0.4 MPa is placed in a solution of Ψ = −0.8 MPa. Water will
o: Move in, then the cell bursts
questions.x: Ψw(cell) = −1.0 + 0.4 = −0.6 MPa, higher than −0.8 MPa of the solution, so water flows out to the lower potential.
questions.trap: Comparing only Ψs (−1.0 < −0.8) suggests water enters.

questions.q: Total CO₂ molecules released from one glucose in the link reaction plus the Krebs cycle is
questions.x: Link reaction: 1 CO₂ per pyruvate × 2 = 2; Krebs: 2 CO₂ per turn × 2 turns = 4; total 6.
questions.trap: 4 counts only the Krebs cycle.

questions.q: For oxalic acid respiring as 2(COOH)₂ + O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O, the respiratory quotient is
questions.x: RQ = CO₂ released / O₂ used = 4/1 = 4. Organic acids, being rich in oxygen, give RQ above one.
questions.trap: 0.25 inverts the ratio (O₂/CO₂).

questions.q: In the F2 of a trihybrid cross (AaBbCc × AaBbCc), the proportion of offspring with genotype AABBCC is
questions.x: Each gene gives AA with probability 1/4: (1/4)³ = 1/64.
questions.trap: 1/27 wrongly uses 1/3 per gene.

questions.q: A DNA molecule of 1000 base pairs has 20% adenine. The number of guanine bases in it is
questions.x: A = T = 20% so G = C = 30% of 2000 bases = 600.
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
questions.trap: 300 takes 30% of 1000 instead of 2000 bases.

questions.q: Genes A and B are 20 map units apart. In a test cross AB/ab × ab/ab, the percentage of Ab offspring is
questions.x: 20 map units = 20% recombinants, shared equally between Ab and aB: 10% each.
questions.trap: 20% is the total of both recombinant classes.

questions.q: A meiocyte with 2n = 20 at pachytene shows
questions.x: 20 chromosomes pair into 10 bivalents; each chromosome has 2 chromatids: 20 × 2 = 40.
questions.trap: 20 chromatids forgets replication in S phase.

questions.q: In an angiosperm with 2n = 24, the chromosome numbers in the endosperm and an antipodal cell are
questions.x: Endosperm is 3n = 36; antipodals are part of the haploid embryo sac, n = 12.
questions.trap: 24 is the nucellus or embryo, not the endosperm.

questions.q: Griffith's experiment, in which heat-killed virulent pneumococci changed live harmless ones into virulent forms, demonstrated
questions.x: A 'transforming principle' from the dead S-strain changed R-strain bacteria into S-strain; Avery and colleagues later showed it was DNA.
questions.trap: Transduction needs a bacteriophage as carrier.

questions.q: Hershey and Chase grew bacteriophages with ³²P and ³⁵S and found that
o: Only ³⁵S-labelled protein entered the bacteria, so protein is the genetic material
Only ³²P-labelled DNA entered the bacteria, so DNA is the genetic material
questions.x: ³²P labels DNA and ³⁵S labels protein. After infection and blending, radioactive phosphorus was inside the bacteria while sulphur stayed in the empty coats outside.
questions.trap: ³⁵S marks the protein coat, which stays outside.

questions.q: In the Watson–Crick (B-form) DNA, the distance between two adjacent base pairs is
questions.x: Each turn is 3.4 nm long and has 10 base pairs, so adjacent pairs are 0.34 nm apart; the helix is 2 nm wide.
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
questions.trap: 3.4 nm is the length of a full turn.

questions.q: A B-form DNA double helix is 68 nm long. The number of base pairs in it is
questions.x: Base pairs = length ÷ 0.34 nm = 68 ÷ 0.34 = 200 (that is 20 complete turns).
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
questions.trap: 20 is the number of turns, not base pairs.

questions.q: The most abundant type of RNA in a cell is
questions.x: rRNA makes up about 80% of cellular RNA because every ribosome is built around it; mRNA is only a few percent.
questions.s: Composition, structure and functions of DNA and RNA
questions.trap: mRNA is the most talked-about, not the most abundant.

questions.q: The enzyme that unwinds the DNA double helix at the replication fork by breaking hydrogen bonds is
questions.x: Helicase separates the strands; primase lays RNA primers, DNA polymerase extends them and ligase seals the nicks.
questions.trap: Ligase joins fragments; it does not unwind.

questions.q: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only to a free 3′-OH end. Therefore new DNA strands always grow in the direction
questions.x: Each new nucleotide is joined to the 3′-OH of the previous one, so synthesis runs 5′ → 3′; this is why the lagging strand forms Okazaki fragments.

questions.q: Bacteria with only ¹⁵N-DNA are grown in a ¹⁴N medium for two generations. The proportion of hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) DNA molecules is
questions.x: Generation 1: both molecules hybrid. Generation 2: each hybrid gives one hybrid and one light molecule, so 2 of 4 = 50% hybrid (semi-conservative replication).
questions.trap: 100% is the answer after only one generation.

questions.q: The central dogma of molecular biology (DNA → RNA → protein) was proposed by
questions.x: Crick (1958) stated that genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein; Temin and Baltimore later found reverse transcription.

questions.q: The genetic code is called degenerate because
o: Most amino acids are coded by more than one codon
One codon codes for several amino acids
questions.x: 61 sense codons code for only 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons (e.g. leucine has 6). Each codon is still unambiguous.
questions.trap: One codon for many amino acids would be ambiguity, which does not occur.

questions.q: Of the 64 codons, the number that code for amino acids is
questions.x: Three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop signals, leaving 61 sense codons; AUG both codes for methionine and starts translation.
questions.trap: 64 forgets the three stop codons.

questions.q: The coding region of an mRNA, from the start codon up to and including the stop codon, has 453 nucleotides. The polypeptide formed has
questions.x: 453 ÷ 3 = 151 codons; the stop codon adds no amino acid, so 151 − 1 = 150 amino acids.
questions.trap: 151 counts the stop codon as an amino acid.

questions.q: A cross between an F1 hybrid and either of its parents is a
questions.x: Any F1 × parent cross is a back cross; when the parent used is the homozygous recessive one, the back cross is also a test cross.
questions.trap: Test cross is only the recessive-parent case.

questions.q: Mendel's law of segregation (purity of gametes) states that
o: Alleles of different genes assort independently
The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets only one
Dominant alleles mask recessive ones in the F1
questions.x: Alleles stay unmixed in the hybrid and separate at meiosis, so every gamete is pure for one allele of each gene.
questions.trap: Independent assortment is the second law, about two genes.

questions.q: In a cross AaBb × aaBb (independent genes), the fraction of offspring with genotype aabb is
questions.x: Aa × aa gives aa with probability 1/2; Bb × Bb gives bb with probability 1/4; 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.
questions.trap: 1/16 assumes both parents are AaBb.

questions.q: When AaBbCc is self-pollinated (independent genes, complete dominance), the fraction of offspring showing all three dominant traits is
questions.x: Each gene gives the dominant phenotype with probability 3/4; (3/4)³ = 27/64.
questions.trap: 1/64 is the fraction homozygous for all three.

questions.q: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt) give 800 offspring. The expected number of heterozygous tall offspring is
questions.x: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; heterozygotes are 2/4 of 800 = 400.
questions.trap: 600 counts all tall plants, including TT.

questions.q: In snapdragon, red × white gives pink F1. A pink plant crossed with a white plant gives
questions.x: Pink (Rr) × white (rr) gives Rr and rr in equal numbers: 1 pink : 1 white.
questions.trap: 1:2:1 is pink × pink.

questions.q: A child has blood group O and the mother has group A. The father CANNOT have blood group
questions.x: An O child is ii, so each parent must pass an i allele. Fathers of group A (Iᴬi), B (Iᴮi) or O (ii) can; an AB father (IᴬIᴮ) has no i.

questions.q: Parents with blood groups AB and O can have children with blood group
questions.x: IᴬIᴮ × ii gives Iᴬi (group A) or Iᴮi (group B), each with probability 1/2; no child can be AB or O.
questions.trap: Children do not simply copy the parents' groups.

questions.q: Crossing over takes place between
o: Sister chromatids of the same chromosome
questions.x: At pachytene, segments are exchanged between non-sister chromatids of a bivalent, giving recombinant chromatids.
questions.s: Concept and significance of crossing over
questions.trap: Sister chromatids are identical, so exchange gives nothing new.

questions.q: A haemophilic man marries a woman who is neither haemophilic nor a carrier. Their children will be
o: All daughters carriers and all sons normal
questions.x: The father passes his Xʰ to every daughter (carriers) and his Y to every son; sons get a normal X from the mother.
questions.trap: Fathers never pass their X to sons.

questions.q: A woman with normal vision whose father was colour-blind marries a colour-blind man. The probability that their daughter is colour-blind is
questions.x: She is a carrier (XᶜX). Daughters receive Xᶜ from the father and Xᶜ or X from the mother, so 1/2 are colour-blind.
questions.trap: 1/4 is the chance for any child, not for a daughter.

questions.q: Genes on the non-homologous part of the Y chromosome, passed only from father to son, are
questions.x: Holandric (Y-linked) genes, such as the one usually cited for hypertrichosis of the ear, appear only in males and pass straight from father to son.
questions.s: Concepts and patterns of sex-linked inheritance

questions.q: Reversal of a chromosome segment by 180° is called
questions.x: Inversion changes gene order within one chromosome; translocation moves a segment to a non-homologous chromosome.
questions.s: Concept and types (gene and chromosomal mutations)

questions.q: Sickle-cell anaemia results from
o: A frameshift that stops globin synthesis
A single base substitution that replaces glutamic acid with valine in β-globin
questions.x: Codon GAG changes to GUG, so the sixth amino acid of β-globin becomes valine instead of glutamic acid; it is a point mutation.
questions.s: Concept and types (gene and chromosomal mutations)

questions.q: A plant species has 2n = 24. A trisomic plant of this species has how many chromosomes in its somatic cells?
questions.x: Trisomy (2n + 1) adds one extra chromosome: 24 + 1 = 25. 36 would be triploid (3n).
questions.s: Causes and examples of genetic disorders
questions.trap: 36 confuses trisomy with triploidy.

questions.q: Cultivated banana and seedless watermelon are seedless mainly because they are
questions.x: With three chromosome sets, homologues cannot pair evenly in meiosis, gametes are unbalanced and seeds fail to form.
questions.trap: Tetraploids are usually fertile.

questions.q: The karyotype of a person with Klinefelter's syndrome is
questions.x: Klinefelter males have an extra X (44 + XXY): tall, sterile, with small testes. 45, XO is Turner's syndrome.
questions.s: Causes and examples of genetic disorders
questions.trap: 45, XO is Turner's syndrome.

questions.q: Albinism is caused by a lack of the enzyme
questions.x: Tyrosinase converts tyrosine towards melanin; an autosomal recessive defect leaves skin, hair and eyes without pigment.
questions.s: Causes and examples of genetic disorders
questions.trap: Phenylalanine hydroxylase is missing in phenylketonuria.

questions.q: For a fully flaccid cell, the diffusion pressure deficit (DPD) equals its
questions.x: DPD = OP − TP. In a flaccid cell TP = 0, so DPD = OP, its maximum value.
questions.trap: Zero is the DPD of a fully turgid cell.

questions.q: Entry of water into a cell placed in a hypotonic solution is
questions.x: Water moves into the cell, which has a lower water potential than the hypotonic solution; the opposite outflow is exosmosis.
questions.s: Water relations: osmosis and its types, plasmolysis

questions.q: In a plasmolysed cell, the space between the cell wall and the shrunken protoplast is filled with
questions.x: The cell wall is freely permeable, so the outside solution passes through it and fills the gap; the plasma membrane is the selective barrier.
questions.s: Water relations: osmosis and its types, plasmolysis

questions.q: A flaccid cell (Ψp = 0) with Ψs = −0.7 MPa is placed in pure water until it stops gaining water. Its pressure potential is then
questions.x: At equilibrium Ψw(cell) = Ψw(pure water) = 0, so Ψp = 0 − (−0.7) = +0.7 MPa (ignoring dilution of the sap).
questions.trap: 0 MPa is the starting value, before water enters.

questions.q: The pressure exerted by the cell wall on the protoplast, equal and opposite to turgor pressure, is
questions.x: When a turgid protoplast presses on the wall (turgor pressure), the elastic wall pushes back with an equal wall pressure.

questions.q: Most of the water lost by transpiration from a leafy plant escapes through
questions.x: Stomatal transpiration accounts for about 90% of water loss; cuticular and lenticular transpiration are minor. Hydathodes give guttation.
questions.trap: Hydathodes release liquid water (guttation), not vapour.

questions.q: Which condition decreases the rate of transpiration?
questions.x: Humid air lowers the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and air, so less water diffuses out; wind, heat and light all increase transpiration.

questions.q: The cohesion–tension (transpiration pull) theory of ascent of sap was proposed by
questions.x: Dixon and Joly (1894) explained that transpiration pulls a continuous water column held together by cohesion and adhesion in xylem.

questions.q: Root pressure, seen as sap oozing from a freshly cut stem, results from
o: Active absorption of mineral ions by roots, drawing water in osmotically
Imbibition by the cell walls of root hairs
questions.x: Root cells pump ions into the xylem using ATP; water follows by osmosis and builds a positive pressure that pushes sap up.
questions.trap: Transpiration pull is a tension, not a pressure from below.

questions.q: Leaves droop on a hot afternoon but recover by evening. This temporary wilting occurs because
o: The soil has no water left at all
Water lost by transpiration exceeds water absorbed
questions.x: In incipient or temporary wilting, transpiration briefly outruns absorption; when transpiration falls in the evening, cells regain turgor.
questions.trap: No soil water would cause permanent wilting.

questions.q: Carotenoids help photosynthesis by
o: Acting as the reaction centre of photosystem I
Absorbing extra wavelengths and protecting chlorophyll from photo-oxidation
questions.x: Carotenes and xanthophylls are accessory pigments: they pass absorbed blue-green light energy to chlorophyll a and quench excess energy.

questions.q: Chlorophyll b differs from chlorophyll a in having
o: An iron atom in place of magnesium
An aldehyde (–CHO) group in place of a methyl (–CH₃) group
questions.x: Both have a Mg-porphyrin head and phytol tail; chlorophyll a carries –CH₃ and chlorophyll b carries –CHO at the same position.
questions.trap: Iron sits in haem, not in chlorophyll.

questions.q: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation
o: Uses both PS I and PS II and yields ATP, NADPH and O₂
Uses only PS I and yields only ATP
Uses only PS II and yields only NADPH
Occurs in the stroma and fixes CO₂
questions.x: Electrons flow from water through PS II and PS I to NADP⁺ (Z-scheme), giving ATP, NADPH and O₂. Cyclic flow uses PS I and gives ATP only.
questions.trap: PS I alone with only ATP is cyclic flow.

questions.q: To release one molecule of O₂ by photolysis of water, the number of electrons removed is
questions.x: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂; the oxygen-evolving complex of PS II passes the four electrons to P680.
questions.trap: 2 electrons release only half an O₂ molecule.

questions.q: How many turns of the Calvin cycle are needed to make one molecule of glucose?
questions.x: Each turn fixes one CO₂; glucose has 6 carbons, so 6 turns (using 18 ATP and 12 NADPH).
questions.trap: 12 is the NADPH count.

questions.q: In C₄ plants, the Calvin cycle takes place in the chloroplasts of
questions.x: Mesophyll cells fix CO₂ into C₄ acids, which release CO₂ in the bundle sheath, where RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle work.
questions.trap: Mesophyll cells only make the C₄ acid.

questions.q: Photorespiration occurs because RuBisCO
o: Is found only in C₄ plants
Also acts as an oxygenase when O₂ is high and CO₂ is low
questions.x: RuBisCO can add O₂ to RuBP, forming phosphoglycolate, which is recycled through peroxisome and mitochondrion with loss of CO₂.

questions.q: Photorespiration is negligible in
questions.x: C₄ plants concentrate CO₂ around RuBisCO in the bundle sheath, so its oxygenase activity is suppressed.
questions.trap: Hot days increase photorespiration in C₃ plants.

questions.q: The law of limiting factors in photosynthesis was given by
questions.x: Blackman (1905): when a process depends on several factors, its rate is limited by the factor nearest its minimum value.

questions.q: In bright light, warming a plant from 15 °C to 25 °C increases photosynthesis, but in dim light it does not. This shows that in dim light
questions.x: By Blackman's law, raising a non-limiting factor has no effect; in dim light, light itself limits the rate, so warmth adds nothing.
questions.trap: Temperature limits only in bright light here.

questions.q: Fruits and vegetables keep longer in cold storage because low temperature
questions.x: Respiration is enzyme-driven; cooling slows it, so stored food is used up more slowly and decay is delayed.

questions.q: The chemiosmotic theory of ATP synthesis was given by
questions.x: Mitchell proposed that electron transport pumps H⁺ across the inner membrane and the H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase drives ATP formation.
questions.s: Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation

questions.q: FADH₂ yields less ATP than NADH in the electron transport system because FADH₂
o: Passes its electrons in at complex II, bypassing one proton-pumping step
Gives its electrons directly to oxygen
questions.x: NADH enters at complex I; FADH₂ enters through complex II, which pumps no protons, so fewer H⁺ are moved and less ATP results.
questions.s: Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation

questions.q: In aerobic respiration of one glucose, the net ATP formed by substrate-level phosphorylation is
questions.x: Glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP and the Krebs cycle 2 (one GTP/ATP per turn × 2 turns); 2 + 2 = 4.
questions.trap: 2 counts only glycolysis.

questions.q: A shoot bends towards unilateral light because auxin
o: Collects on the lit side and makes those cells elongate more
Collects on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more
Is destroyed on both sides equally
questions.x: Light causes auxin to move laterally to the shaded side; faster elongation there curves the stem towards light (phototropism).

questions.q: Gibberellins were first discovered from the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi, which causes
questions.x: Kurosawa found that infected rice seedlings grow abnormally tall because the fungus secretes gibberellin.

questions.q: Kinetin, the first cytokinin discovered, was isolated by Skoog and Miller from
questions.x: Kinetin (6-furfurylaminopurine) was obtained from degraded herring sperm DNA; zeatin, the first natural cytokinin, came from maize.
questions.trap: Zeatin came from corn, not kinetin.

questions.q: In tissue culture, a high cytokinin-to-auxin ratio in the medium favours
questions.x: Skoog and Miller showed high cytokinin : auxin gives shoots, high auxin : cytokinin gives roots, and balanced levels give callus.
questions.trap: High auxin, not cytokinin, favours roots.

questions.q: Which seed shows epigeal germination?
questions.x: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above ground (castor, bean, cotton). Pea, gram and maize are hypogeal.

questions.q: Keeping moist seeds at low temperature for some weeks to break their dormancy is called
questions.x: Cold, moist stratification removes inhibitors and ends embryo dormancy; scarification breaks a hard seed coat.
questions.trap: Vernalisation is cold treatment to induce flowering.

questions.q: The cell theory was formulated by
questions.x: Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Schwann (animals, 1839) stated that all living things are made of cells; Virchow added that cells come from cells.
questions.trap: Hooke only named the cell.

questions.q: Which structure is present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
questions.x: All cells need ribosomes to make proteins (70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotic cytoplasm); membrane-bound organelles are absent in prokaryotes.
questions.s: Concept of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

questions.q: Histone proteins packing DNA into nucleosomes are absent in
questions.x: Eukaryotic DNA wraps around histone octamers to form nucleosomes; bacterial DNA is naked and lies in the nucleoid.
questions.s: Concept of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

questions.q: The secondary wall of a plant cell is laid down
o: Inside the primary wall after the cell stops enlarging
questions.x: Order from outside: middle lamella → primary wall → secondary wall. The thick, often lignified secondary wall is added inside once growth stops.

questions.q: Movement of ions across a membrane against their concentration gradient using ATP is
questions.x: Carrier pumps such as the Na⁺/K⁺ pump spend ATP to move solutes uphill; diffusion and osmosis go downhill without energy.

questions.q: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane are called
questions.x: Cristae increase the surface for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase; thylakoids and grana belong to chloroplasts.

questions.q: The stalked F₁ particles (oxysomes) that make ATP are located on the
questions.x: F₀–F₁ ATP synthase sits in the inner membrane with the F₁ head projecting into the matrix.

questions.q: Stacks of thylakoids inside a chloroplast are called
questions.x: Thylakoids pile up like coins to form grana, linked by stroma lamellae; the light reactions occur on their membranes.

questions.q: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are believed to have arisen from free-living prokaryotes. This idea is the
questions.x: Their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and double membranes support the idea that they were once engulfed bacteria.

questions.q: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is mainly concerned with
o: Synthesis of proteins for secretion and membranes
questions.x: Ribosomes on RER make proteins that enter its lumen for folding and transport to the Golgi; smooth ER makes lipids.
questions.trap: Lipid and steroid synthesis is smooth ER.

questions.q: In plant cells, the Golgi apparatus occurs as many scattered units called
questions.x: Each dictyosome is a stack of flattened cisternae; they supply vesicles for the cell plate and cell-wall polysaccharides.

questions.q: Lysosomal hydrolytic enzymes work best at
questions.x: A proton pump keeps the lysosome interior acidic; its acid hydrolases (proteases, lipases, nucleases) are active there.

questions.q: The nucleolus is the site of synthesis of
questions.x: The nucleolus forms at the nucleolar organiser; it transcribes rRNA and assembles it with proteins into ribosomal subunits.

questions.q: The basal body of a cilium has microtubules arranged as
o: Nine peripheral triplets with none in the centre (9 + 0)
Nine doublets with two central singlets (9 + 2)
questions.x: Basal bodies, like centrioles, have a 9 + 0 triplet arrangement; the axoneme growing from them is 9 + 2.
questions.trap: 9 + 2 is the axoneme, not the basal body.

questions.q: Raphides, needle-shaped crystals in plant cells such as those of Colocasia, are made of
questions.x: Raphides are bundles of calcium oxalate needles; cystoliths of Ficus leaves are calcium carbonate.
questions.trap: Calcium carbonate forms cystoliths.

questions.q: Aleurone grains stored in seeds are made of
questions.x: Aleurone grains are protein bodies, e.g. in the aleurone layer of cereals, which secretes amylase during germination.

questions.q: A cell in G₁ has 2C DNA. Its DNA content in G₂ is
questions.x: DNA doubles during S phase, so G₂ cells have 4C; the chromosome number stays the same.

questions.q: Chromosomes are best counted and studied at
questions.x: At metaphase chromosomes are maximally condensed and lined up on the equatorial plate, so their number and shape are clearest.

questions.q: Chiasmata first become visible during
questions.x: Crossing over happens at pachytene, but homologues begin to separate at diplotene, revealing the chiasmata where exchange occurred.
questions.trap: Crossing over is at pachytene; chiasmata are seen later.

questions.q: A cell with 2n = 18 completes meiosis I. Each daughter cell has
questions.x: Homologues separate at anaphase I, so each cell gets n = 9 chromosomes, but each still has two sister chromatids: 18 chromatids.
questions.trap: 9 chromatids forgets chromatids separate only in meiosis II.

questions.q: Inulin, stored in tubers of dahlia, is a polymer of
questions.x: Inulin is a fructan, a polysaccharide of fructose units; starch, glycogen and cellulose are glucose polymers.
questions.trap: Most storage polysaccharides are glucose, but not inulin.

questions.q: Glucose and fructose are both C₆H₁₂O₆, but fructose is a
questions.x: Glucose has an aldehyde group (aldohexose); fructose has a keto group at C-2 (ketohexose).

questions.q: Phospholipids form the bilayer of cell membranes because each molecule has
o: A hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails
questions.x: Amphipathic phospholipids turn their heads towards water and tails inwards, forming a bilayer spontaneously.

questions.q: A simple fat (triglyceride) is formed from
o: Three glycerols and one fatty acid
One glycerol and three fatty acids
questions.x: Three fatty acids form ester bonds with the three –OH groups of glycerol, releasing three water molecules.

questions.q: Deficiency symptoms of nitrogen and magnesium appear first in older leaves because these elements are
o: Immobile and fixed in older leaves
Mobile and moved to younger leaves
questions.x: Mobile nutrients (N, P, K, Mg) are withdrawn from older leaves to growing parts, so old leaves turn yellow first; immobile Ca shows in young leaves.

questions.q: Zinc is needed for the synthesis of auxin because it is required to make its precursor
questions.x: IAA is made from the amino acid tryptophan, and zinc is needed for tryptophan synthesis; zinc deficiency causes little-leaf and rosetting.

questions.q: An apoenzyme together with its cofactor forms the
questions.x: Apoenzyme (protein part) + cofactor (metal ion, coenzyme or prosthetic group) = active holoenzyme.

questions.q: Ribozymes are biological catalysts made of
questions.x: Ribozymes are catalytic RNAs, e.g. the peptidyl transferase activity of ribosomal RNA; they show that not all enzymes are proteins.

questions.q: Bryophyllum reproduces vegetatively by
o: Adventitious buds on the leaf margins
questions.x: Notches on Bryophyllum leaf margins bear adventitious buds that grow into new plantlets.

questions.q: Of the four megaspores formed by meiosis in most angiosperms,
o: The chalazal one is functional and the other three degenerate
The micropylar one is functional and the other three degenerate
Two fuse to form the egg
questions.x: In monosporic (Polygonum-type) development, the chalazal megaspore enlarges into the embryo sac; the three nearer the micropyle degenerate.
questions.trap: The micropylar megaspore usually degenerates.

questions.q: The filiform apparatus, which guides the pollen tube into the embryo sac, is found in the
questions.x: Finger-like wall ingrowths at the micropylar tip of the synergids secrete chemicals that attract the pollen tube.

questions.q: Pollination by water, as in Vallisneria, is called
questions.x: Vallisneria male flowers float to the surface and reach the female flowers on long stalks; water carries the pollen.

questions.q: Wind-pollinated flowers usually have
o: Light, dry pollen and large feathery stigmas
questions.x: Anemophilous flowers (maize, grasses) produce plenty of light, smooth pollen and expose feathery stigmas to catch it; colour, scent and nectar are wasted.
questions.trap: Bright petals and nectar suit insect pollination.

questions.q: In a monocot (grass) embryo, the protective sheath covering the plumule is the
questions.x: The coleoptile sheathes the plumule; the coleorhiza sheathes the radicle; the scutellum is the single cotyledon.
questions.s: Structure of monocot and dicot embryo
questions.trap: Coleorhiza covers the radicle.

questions.q: A synergid of an angiosperm has 8 chromosomes. The endosperm and zygote will have, respectively,
questions.x: Synergids are haploid, so n = 8. Endosperm is 3n = 24 (two polar nuclei + one male gamete); the zygote is 2n = 16.
